content.title: About
content.content: Beet greens are the edible leaves of the beet plant (Beta vulgaris). When cooked they retain a vivid green color, a tender texture and a mildly sweet, earthy flavor. They are commonly used in soups, stews, salads and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beet greens are rich in chlorophyll, which gives them their deep green hue.
Traditional cuisines of Eastern Europe (Russia, Ukraine, Poland) often feature beet greens in soups such as shchi or added to borscht.
The leaves can also be used as animal feed, but are prized for human consumption because of their high vitamin content.
Nitrate levels in the leaves can be high, so cooking is recommended to reduce them.
Beet greens are sometimes confused with spinach, yet they have a stronger, slightly bitter taste.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and supports bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These compounds promote eye health, immune function and protect skin from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and enhances iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: High in minerals
items.content: Beet greens provide calcium, magnesium, iron and potassium, which are important for muscle, nerve and cardiovascular function.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, supports satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: Beet greens can accumulate nitrates, especially when grown with intensive fertilization. Blanching or cooking reduces nitrate levels.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: The leaves contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to beet greens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beet greens can be blanched, sautéed, added to soups or stews, or quickly stir‑fried with garlic and onion. They also work well pureed or as a filling for pies. Before cooking, rinse the leaves thoroughly and trim off thick stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh leaves in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or wrapped in a damp towel for up to 3‑5 days. Cooked greens should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Breakfast bar, NFS is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast bar containing whole grains, nuts, dried fruit and added vitamins. It is designed for a quick on‑the‑go snack, providing energy and nutrients during the first hours of the day.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS bars are made from whole oat flakes, preserving most of the dietary fiber.
They contain extracts of acai and blueberry berries, rich in antioxidants.
Each bar provides about 15 g of plant‑based protein from pea protein isolate.
The product is gluten‑free, suitable for people with celiac disease.
Packaging is made from recyclable material in line with sustainability principles.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: The mix of complex carbs and protein delivers a steady energy release without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grains and dried fruit supply dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Added B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berry extracts help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Sugar is replaced with natural sweeteners, making the bar suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Contains almonds and cashews, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: One bar contains roughly 200 kcal, so it should fit within your daily energy budget.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Some variants include guarana extract, which adds a small amount of caffeine.

items.title: Sugar level
items.content: Although reduced, people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is ready to eat straight from the pack. It is convenient to carry in a bag, at work or the gym. For extra bulk you can crumble it into yogurt, smoothies or oatmeal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly to maintain crunchiness. For long‑term storage (over 6 months) keep refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese spread made from Swiss cheese is a smooth, creamy product with a characteristic nutty aroma. It is produced from selected Swiss cheese, cream, and a touch of spices, making it an ideal base for sandwiches, appetizers, and various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Swiss cheese is known for its mild flavor and distinctive "holes" formed during fermentation.
Cheese spread is often used as a base for fondue and hot sandwiches.
Additional ingredients such as garlic, herbs, or mustard may be added for flavor variations.
Traditionally, Swiss cheese is made from cow's milk, though goat or sheep milk versions exist.
Cheese spread can be kept refrigerated for up to 2 weeks after opening.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Swiss cheese provides high levels of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The spread supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that may benefit heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermentation of the cheese creates beneficial bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: High salt content
items.content: The spread can be salty; people monitoring sodium intake should use it sparingly.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: May cause reactions in those allergic to dairy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised for weight‑managed diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread can be applied to bread, crackers, used as a filling for wraps, mixed into sauces, casseroles, and salads. It also pairs well with vegetable sticks or fruit for a contrasting taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the spread refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. After opening, consume within 10‑14 days. Do not freeze, as texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: The multigrain high‑fiber cookie is made from a blend of whole grains, oats, bran, and sunflower seeds. It has a crunchy texture, mild sweetness, and a rich nutty aroma. The product is suitable for a daily snack and can be incorporated into diets that emphasize fiber intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cookie contains five different whole grains, making it more nutritious than typical sweet cookies.
Its fiber content supports a healthy gut microbiome.
No artificial colors or flavors are used.
It is vegetarian‑friendly but not gluten‑free.
Each serving (30 g) provides over 5 g of dietary fiber.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: High fiber promotes regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Soluble fiber from oats can help reduce LDL ("bad") cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sustained satiety
items.content: Fiber slows carbohydrate absorption, keeping you feeling full longer.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The multigrain blend provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Sunflower seeds and bran are rich in vitamin E and phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to grains or seeds
items.content: The product may contain traces of wheat, oats, and sunflower seeds, which should be considered by individuals with relevant allergies.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite its high fiber, the cookie contains added sugar; people monitoring blood glucose should account for it.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cookie is relatively calorie‑dense (about 150 kcal per 30 g), so moderation is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt, kefir, or muesli, or use it as a crunchy base for desserts. For a softer texture, lightly warm it in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to maintain crunch and prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Corned beef hash is a dish made from finely chopped cooked beef (usually canned), potatoes and onions, fried until a golden crust forms. It is often served with a fried egg or scrambled eggs and works as a hearty breakfast or lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “corned beef” comes from the large salt crystals (“corns”) used to cure the meat.
Originally the hash was a way to use leftover meat from holiday meals so it wouldn’t go to waste.
In the United States corned beef hash became popular in the early 20th century as a quick meal for laborers.
Many variations exist, adding bell peppers, carrots, beans or even cheese.
In some regions it is served with maple syrup for a sweet‑salty contrast.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Energy‑dense
items.content: The combination of protein and carbohydrates offers sustained satiety and energy.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc aids immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned corned beef often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A significant amount of saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels if eaten frequently.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Possible preservatives
items.content: Certain canned versions contain additives that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hash hot, either on its own or topped with a fried or scrambled egg, sour cream, or tomato sauce. It pairs well with toast, bread, or a fresh vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened jar of corned beef hash in the refrigerator for up to 5 days after opening. Portions can be frozen in airtight containers for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Goldfish crackers are small fish‑shaped snacks coated with a savory cheese glaze. Made from wheat flour, vegetable oils and cheese, they have a crunchy texture and a light, slightly salty cheese flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Goldfish were first introduced in the United States in 1962 by Pepperidge Farm.
The fish shape was chosen to make the product instantly recognizable and appealing to children.
More than 20 Goldfish flavors exist, including original cheese, pizza, barbecue and sweet varieties.
In the 2020s the company launched gluten‑free and dairy‑free versions for people with dietary restrictions.
A typical bag contains about 30‑40 pieces, making it a convenient on‑the‑go snack.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Goldfish provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains vitamin B2
items.content: The cheese coating supplies a modest amount of riboflavin, which supports energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Wheat flour contributes iron, an essential mineral for blood formation.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: Their crunchy texture and bite‑size shape make them a handy snack between meals.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat and cheese, which can trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: Cheese‑flavored crackers are often salty; excessive sodium intake may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although portions are small, Goldfish are relatively calorie‑dense, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The small fish shapes can pose a choking risk for young children and should be given under supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Goldfish are perfect straight from the bag, can be added to salads, soups, or used as a garnish. They pair well with dips, yogurt or cheese spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. For longer shelf life keep them in an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

ice-cream-chocolate-with-additional-ingr.title: Chocolate Ice Cream with Additional Ingredients

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate ice cream with additional ingredients is a creamy frozen dessert made from milk, cream, and sugar, flavored with cocoa butter and often enriched with nuts, fruit pieces, cookies or caramel. It offers a rich chocolate taste, smooth texture, and can contain up to 432 different add‑ins, creating a wide range of flavor combinations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate ice cream first appeared in the late 19th century when cocoa butter began to be used in frozen desserts.
The first commercial chocolate ice cream was sold in the United States in 1895.
Adding nuts and dried fruits increases the content of healthy fats and vitamins.
In some countries the dessert is served as soft‑serve, where a higher temperature and air incorporation create a lighter texture.
There are more than 400 flavor pairings when various toppings are mixed into the base chocolate ice cream.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa butter contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals and support heart health.

items.title: Calcium enrichment
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream supply vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Nutrient‑dense add‑ins
items.content: Additional ingredients such as nuts, seeds, and dried fruit add protein, fiber, and healthy fats.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin and endorphin production, helping to lift mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large servings can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort from the dairy base.

items.title: Allergy to nuts and other add‑ins
items.content: Some toppings (peanuts, almonds, cashews) can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cream and chocolate increase saturated fat levels, which may be undesirable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Cold sensitivity
items.content: Eating ice cream can cause "brain freeze" in individuals sensitive to cold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ice cream in bowls, cones, or waffle cups. Top with fresh fruit, nuts, chocolate shavings, caramel sauce, or sprinkle with spices such as cinnamon or ginger. For a lighter version, mix in a scoop of sugar‑free ice cream or replace part of the cream with plant‑based milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C in an airtight container to prevent ice crystal formation. Over long storage the flavor and texture may change; it is best consumed within 2–3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) is a leafy cruciferous vegetable renowned for its high nutrient density. The frozen, cooked, fat‑added product is a ready‑to‑eat side dish that retains most of the vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale is often called a “superfood” because of its rich micronutrient profile.
It contains more vitamin K than spinach by several folds.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of its antioxidants, which can degrade in fresh kale during long storage.
Traditionally, Scandinavians cooked kale with lard or butter to improve flavor and texture.
Kale can be used as a rice substitute in low‑carb diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High antioxidant content
items.content: Kale provides vitamin C, beta‑carotene and flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Its fiber promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Kale supplies calcium, magnesium and iron, important for bones, muscles and blood formation.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and low sodium levels help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Kale contains glucosinolates, which in large amounts may affect thyroid function.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to Brassicaceae vegetables.

items.title: Added fat content
items.content: Because the product already includes fat, people monitoring calories should account for it in their daily intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen portion in a skillet or microwave, stirring to distribute the added fat evenly. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or mixed into vegetable medleys. Enhance flavor with herbs, garlic or a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, consume within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Grilled shrimp have a tender flesh, a light smoky aroma, and a naturally sweet flavor. They are high‑protein, low‑calorie, and provide essential minerals such as iodine, zinc, and selenium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp belong to the crustacean family and are among the most consumed seafood worldwide.
Grilling preserves most nutrients while adding a distinctive charred flavor.
There are over 2,000 shrimp species, but tiger and white shrimp are most common in cuisine.
Shrimp can change shell color depending on water temperature and growth stage.
In Japan, grilled shrimp are often served with soy sauce and wasabi.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of grilled shrimp provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The same serving contains roughly 90 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly option.

items.title: Source of iodine
items.content: Iodine supports thyroid function and hormonal balance.

items.title: Contains omega‑3s
items.content: Shrimp supply modest amounts of EPA and DHA, beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Astaxanthin, present in shrimp, helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, requiring medical attention.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: In certain regions shrimp can accumulate cadmium or mercury, so choose reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow bacterial growth leading to food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled shrimp can be enjoyed as a standalone appetizer, added to salads, pastas, rice dishes, or used in sandwiches. They are easy to eat with fingers, or can be sliced for incorporation into hot meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shrimp in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen shrimp store at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen shrimp in the fridge before cooking, and store cooked grilled shrimp in an airtight container for no more than 24 hours.
